Chapter 2: Trapped by Tradition—The Shift from Guest to Prisoner
Have you ever noticed how, sometimes, a situation you thought was just a rough patch suddenly becomes your new reality? That’s exactly what happened to this American mother and her daughter.
At first, there were only hints—quiet changes that you might brush off if you weren’t paying close attention. The husband, who once talked about going home, started dodging the topic. Family members, who’d seemed so welcoming, now insisted they needed to stay. They talked about responsibility, about family ties, and painted the world outside as something dangerous.
The air itself started to feel heavier, like the walls were closing in, even if nothing was said out loud.
Then, without any warning, the real shock came. The husband sat them down and told them—just like that—they weren’t going back to America. Iran was their home now, and their daughter would grow up with Iranian traditions.
Imagine trying to protest, only to be met with anger and threats. Suddenly, every decision—about her own life, about her child—was out of her hands. The law, the family, even society seemed to be on the husband’s side.
Most of us can’t really imagine what it feels like to have all our choices taken away in a single moment. But for this woman, it was real. Her passport? Gone. Every move she made was watched. She couldn’t leave the house unless someone was with her. Even reaching out for help—calling the American embassy, or even just confiding in someone—was dangerous.
And it wasn’t just her. Her daughter, who’d always been lively and independent, started to shrink inward. She clung to her mom, picking up on all the tension and uncertainty. Even the simple routines—meals, prayers, visits with family—became ways to reinforce control, reminders that their world had changed.
The mother did everything she could to reason with her husband, hoping he’d remember his promises or show some compassion. But he stood firm, convinced that he was doing the right thing for his family. He leaned on religion, tradition, and what the community expected of him. Any attempt to push back was met with threats, including taking her daughter away.
Her world shrank down to the walls of her in-laws’ home. She was always under someone’s watchful eye, and even the smallest acts—like speaking English, or leaving off the veil—were met with punishment. The message was impossible to miss: she wasn’t a guest anymore. She was a prisoner.
Still, even surrounded by fear and isolation, she refused to give up hope. She started watching everything more closely, looking for cracks in the system that trapped her. She listened to conversations, noticed routines, and quietly searched for allies. And she discovered that, while the law was against her, not everyone agreed with how she was being treated. Here and there, a neighbor or distant relative would offer a small kindness—a quick, encouraging word, or just a sympathetic look.
She also learned to hide her true feelings, putting on a compliant face while holding onto a fierce determination inside. She comforted her daughter, whispering that they’d find a way out. Every day turned into a test of her endurance—a battle to keep hope alive, even when everything seemed stacked against her.
It’s easy to underestimate how powerful those little acts of resistance can be. In a world where almost every choice is made for you, just deciding not to give up hope is an act of defiance. And for this mother, that hope grew stronger every day, fueled by her love for her daughter—and her refusal to accept a life of submission.
